title: A Victory and a Terrible Vow
overview: An outcast is called back to lead Gilead against the Ammonites, wins, and then keeps a reckless vow that costs him his only daughter.

parts.label: Rejected, then recruited (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: Because his mother was a prostitute, Jephthah's half brothers drove him out so he would inherit nothing, and in the land of Tob he led a band of men with nothing to lose. When the Ammonites attacked, the elders of Gilead, his home region, asked him to command them, and when he asked whether he would truly stay their head afterward, they called on the LORD as witness to their promise.

parts.label: Arguing before fighting (vv. 12-28)
parts.note: Before any battle, Jephthah answers the Ammonite king's claim to the land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers: Israel took it from Sihon, an Amorite king who attacked them, and has held it unchallenged for 300 years. He adds that each people keeps what its god gives it, naming Chemosh, a god usually linked with Moab rather than Ammon (scholars explain this in different ways), but the king ignores him.

parts.label: The vow and the victory (vv. 29-33)
parts.note: After the Spirit of the LORD comes on him, Jephthah adds a vow of his own: if he wins, whatever comes out of his house to meet him will be a burnt offering, killed and burned whole on an altar. The Hebrew can mean 'whatever' or 'whoever', so readers debate whether he pictured an animal or a person, and he then defeats the Ammonites across twenty towns.

parts.label: His daughter comes out (vv. 34-36)
parts.note: His only child comes out first, dancing with tambourines, the way women welcomed victors home. He tears his clothes in grief and speaks as if she has brought him down, and she tells him to keep his word to the LORD, who has given him victory.

parts.label: The vow carried out (vv. 37-39)
parts.note: She spends two months in the hills with her friends, mourning that she will never marry, and when she returns the text says only that he carried out his vow and that she had never been with a man. Many Jewish and Christian readers, ancient and modern, take this to mean he killed her as a sacrifice, which Israel's law elsewhere forbids, while others argue she was given to lifelong unmarried service, which would explain why her virginity is stressed.

parts.label: Remembered every year (vv. 39-40)
parts.note: Her story became a custom, with Israel's young women going out for four days each year to honor her. The Hebrew verb is uncertain: translations say 'commemorate' or 'celebrate', some scholars suggest 'lament', and a few read 'talk with her', which would mean she was still alive.

disagreement: Christians differ over what Jephthah finally did: many, along with much ancient Jewish tradition, read verse 39 as meaning he sacrificed his daughter, while others read the joining word in verse 31 as 'or' rather than 'and' (both translations here have 'and') and conclude she was dedicated to the LORD as an unmarried woman for life.
think: Is there a point where keeping a promise becomes worse than breaking it, and how would you recognize that point?
